arXiv:2305.09775v1 [math.AP] 16 May 2023

Fast-reaction limits for predator–prey reaction–diffusion systems: improved convergence

Cinzia Soresina    Bao Quoc Tang ††thanks: Corresponding author.
Email addresses: cinzia.soresina@uni-graz.at, quoc.tang@uni-graz.at, bao-ngoc.tran@uni-graz.at    Bao-Ngoc Tran Affiliation: Institute for Mathematics and Scientific Computing, University of Graz, Graz, Austria Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Nong Lam University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
Abstract

The fast-reaction limit for reaction–diffusion systems modelling predator–prey interactions is investigated. In the considered model, predators exist in two possible states, namely searching and handling. The switching rate between these two states happens on a much faster time scale than other processes, leading to the consideration of the fast-reaction limit for the corresponding systems. The rigorous convergence of the solution to the fast-reaction system to the ones of the limiting cross-diffusion system has been recently studied in [Conforto, Desvillettes, Soresina, NoDEA, 25(3):24, 2018]. In this paper, we extend these results by proving improved convergence of solutions and slow manifolds. In particular, we prove that the slow manifold converges strongly in all dimensions without additional assumptions, thanks to use of a modified energy function. This consists in a unified approach since it is applicable to both types of fast-reaction systems, namely with the Lotka–Volterra and the Holling-type II terms.

Keywords: Fast-reaction limit; Predator–prey models; Reaction–diffusion systems; Energy method; Slow manifold.

1 Introduction

An interesting modelling issue in several contexts is the derivation of cross-diffusion terms via Quasi-Steady-State Approximation (QSSA) from a fast-reaction model involving different time scales and standard diffusion. In fact, the justification of cross-diffusion terms from semilinear reaction–didffusion systems including fast-reactions and linear diffusion is fundamental to the understanding of the hidden processes that cross-diffusion terms can describe. It is extremely interesting to identify such fast processes at the microscopic level (in terms of time scales) and to obtain the macroscopic limiting system in which these fast processes are naturally incorporated either in the reaction or in the nonlinear diffusion. In [IMN06], this approach has been exploited to justify the well-known cross-diffusion SKT model for competing species, by considering an instantaneous (fast) conversion between two subpopulations or states. Recently, the fast dichotomy dynamics has been applied to predator–prey interactions [CDS18, DS19, IIK], aggregation phenomena in biology [EIMT22, FIMU12], hunter–gatherers and farmers in Neolithic transition [EHMM21], evolution of dietary diversity and starvation effects [BCDK21], autotoxicity effects in plant growth dynamics [GIS], and behavioural epidemiology [BS].

Althought the QSSA can be performed at a formal level, a proper analysis of the convergence of solutions to the fast-reaction system to the limiting cross-diffusion one is challenging and needs sophisticated techniques [CD14, DT15, CDS18, KS23, TT23]. This paper is devoted to study the fast-reaction limit of the following predator–prey model incorporating competition among predators, proposed in [CDS18]. Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, be a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, e.g. ∂Ω\partial\Omega is of class C2+κC^{2+\kappa} for some κ>0\kappa>0. The model writes

where Nε≥0N^{\varepsilon}\geq 0 denotes the prey population density, psε≥0p_{s}^{\varepsilon}\geq 0 and phε≥0p_{h}^{\varepsilon}\geq 0 the population densities of searching and handling predators, respectively. Assuming that the populations are confined on the domain, system (1) is subjected to homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions

(5) Nε​(x,0)=Ni​n​(x),phε​(x,0)=ph,i​n​(x),psε​(x,0)=ps,i​n​(x),x∈Ω.N^{\varepsilon}(x,0)=N_{in}(x),\quad p_{h}^{\varepsilon}(x,0)=p_{h,in}(x),\quad p_{s}^{\varepsilon}(x,0)=p_{s,in}(x),\quad x\in\Omega.

Here, parameters d1,d2,d3d_{1},\,d_{2},\,d_{3} are the diffusion coefficients of prey, searching, and handling predators, respectively. We assume that handling predators move less far than searching predators, yielding the biologically meaningful constraint on the diffusion coefficients d3<d2d_{3}<d_{2}. In the prey equation, the prey-growth is modelled by a logistic term with maximum growth rate r0r_{0} and carrying capacity 1/η1/\eta, while we have a loss term due to predation. This term involves the parameter α\alpha (attack rate) and parameter ξ\xi, which measures the competition among predators for prey. The mortality rate μ\mu is assumed to be the same for both types of predators and only handling predators give rise, with birth rate Γ\Gamma, to searching predators. We also suppose that there is a conversion (or switch) between the two states: a searching predator becomes handling when encountering a prey and comes back to the searching state after a certain amount of time 1/γ1/\gamma. Furthermore, we assume d1,d2,d3,r0,η,α,γ,Γ,μ>0d_{1},\,d_{2},\,d_{3},\,r_{0},\,\eta,\,\alpha,\,\gamma,\,\Gamma,\,\mu>0  and ξ≥0\xi\geq 0. Note that, for ξ=0\xi=0, we have no competition effect for prey among predators and the predation and switching terms reduce to the Lotka–Volterra type. Under the assumption that the searching–handling switch happens on a much faster time scale than the reproduction and mortality processes, we have that 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1.

As ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0, in some suitable sense, we formally expect that the switching dynamics reaches a quasi-steady-state, namely

subject boundary conditions (10) and initial data (11). From the modelling point of view, the limiting systems inherit and naturally incorporate in the cross-diffusion terms the istantaneous switch between the two predator states. A by-product is the appearence of nonlinear functional responses in the reaction part: we obtain a (prey-dependent) Holling-type II and a (predator-dependent) Beddington–DeAngelis-like functional response, if ξ=0\xi=0 and ξ>0\xi>0, respectively. A sketch of the compartments in the fast-reaction systems and in the limiting system is shown in Figure 1.

These formal limits have been proven rigorously in [CDS18]. More precisely, the following results were obtained.

In the case ξ>0\xi>0, thanks to the strong convergences in Theorem 1.1 (a), we can in fact obtain the strong convergence of the slow manifold, up to a subsequence,

instead of just a distributional convergence in (14). Similarly, this strong convergence can be shown in the case ξ=0\xi=0 and low dimension d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}, see [CDS18, Eq. (55)]. This improved convergence is much more subtle in the case ξ=0\xi=0 and d≥3d\geq 3, since we have no strong convergence of phεp_{h}^{\varepsilon} and psεp_{s}^{\varepsilon}.

In this paper, by using a modified energy method, we show the strong convergence to zero of slow manifold in all dimensions without additional assumptions. This is inspired by the recent work [TT23], where this technique was exploited to prove rigorous derivation of Michaelis–Menten kinetics for reaction–diffusion systems modelling enzyme reactions. In addition, we prove improved convergence results with respect to Theorem 1.1. More precisely, we obtain the following results.

Theorem 1.2 improves the results of Theorem 1.1 by showing the strong convergence of the slow manifold (17) in the case ξ=0\xi=0 in all dimensions, the strong convergence of phε,psεp_{h}^{\varepsilon},p_{s}^{\varepsilon} in (16) for all q∈[1,∞)q\in[1,\infty), and the conditional strong convergence of phε,psεp_{h}^{\varepsilon},p_{s}^{\varepsilon} in (19) under (18). The core idea of our technique to prove Theorem 1.2 is to consider a modified energy function

When ξ=0\xi=0, by taking β=0\beta=0 and p=2p=2, the energy function (20) reduces, up to a multiplication factor, to the function used in [CDS18, Page 15]. The main advantage of having the modification Nε​(x,t)+β⁡(ε)N^{\varepsilon}(x,t)+\beta(\varepsilon) is that it circumvents the problem of lacking a lower bound of Nε​(x,t)N^{\varepsilon}(x,t) in dimensions d≥3d\geq 3. We also remark that this technique is suitable to treat both cases ξ>0\xi>0 and ξ=0\xi=0, corresponding to Lotka–Volterra and Holling-type II terms in the fast-reaction systems, respectively, and therefore it consitutes, to some extent, a unified approach.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, we prove a priori estimates using the modified energy functional Hε​(ε)H^{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon) and the ε\varepsilon-uniform for the solution., while Section 3 is devoted to improved convergence results in both cases ξ>0\xi>0 and ξ=0\xi=0. In the Appendix A, two useful Lemmas are reported for the reader’s convenience.

2 Energy and ε\varepsilon-uniform estimates

In order to rigorously prove the convergence to the slow manifold as well as the convergence to the limiting system given in Theorem 1.2, we first need a priori estimates via the modified energy functional Hε​(t)H^{\varepsilon}(t) defined by (20), provided by Lemma 1, and then ε\varepsilon-uniform estimates for the solution, achieved in Lemma 2.

This section is devoted to the improved convergence results provided by Theorem 1.2 in both cases ξ>0\xi>0 and ξ=0\xi=0, where the latter is more difficult. For the sake of convenience, we will not recall in the statements the assumption on initial data in Theorem 1.2, which are Ni​n∈W2,q​(Ω)N_{in}\in W^{2,q}(\Omega) for q>N+2q>N+2, and ph,i​n,ps,i​n∈L2+δ​(Ω)p_{h,in},p_{s,in}\in L^{2+\delta}(\Omega) for δ>0\delta>0, as well as we always let (Nε,psε,phε)(N^{\varepsilon},p_{s}^{\varepsilon},p_{h}^{\varepsilon}) be the solution to (1) for ε>0\varepsilon>0.

for some constants a,b>0a,\,b>0. If

(40) |a−b|a+b​Cq′𝖬𝖱<1,\displaystyle\frac{|a-b|}{a+b}C_{q^{\prime}}^{\mathsf{MR}}<1,
